**Pitfall**: Standard Newton-Raphson may fail if uniformly distributed seeds are not close to the solution [S1, book].

The claim states that standard Newton-Raphson may fail if uniformly distributed seeds are not close to the solution. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states: 'However, uniformly distributed seeds may not be close to the solution and NR may fail, leading to poor sampling.' It sets itself apart from pure image-order ray casting by performing root finding in object space first, using gradient integration to guide seeds to the surface, thereby ensuring the subsequent directional Newton-Raphson steps converge reliably [S1, book].

The claim states that the method sets itself apart from pure image-order ray casting by performing root finding in object space first, using gradient integration to guide seeds to the surface, and then using directional Newton-Raphson steps. Source [S1] explicitly describes a two-phase process: Phase 1 (Object Space) involves distributing seeds, guiding them via gradient integration to get closer to the isosurface, and then applying Directional Newton-Raphson to refine the projection. Phase 2 (Image Space) uses the results from Phase 1 (surface-tangent quads) as starting points for ray casting. The text confirms that gradient integration is used to mitigate the failure of standard Newton-Raphson when seeds are not close to the solution, ensuring reliable convergence for the subsequent steps. Thus, every fact in the claim is present in the evidence.

To mitigate the failure of Newton-Raphson when starting points are far from the solution, seeds are guided along the gradient field towards the isosurface [S1, book].

The claim states that seeds are guided along the gradient field towards the isosurface to mitigate Newton-Raphson failure when starting points are far from the solution. Source [S1] explicitly states: 'Standard Newton-Raphson may fail if uniformly distributed seeds are not close to the solution. Guiding seeds via gradient integration mitigates this by ensuring starting points are closer to the isosurface.' It further details the process: 'First, uniformly distributed seeds are guided along the gradient field via integration to get closer to the isosurface. Second, Directional Newton-Raphson (NR) is applied to refine the projection onto the isosurface.' This confirms every part of the claim.
